Chapter 42

End to end: the built server, two viewports, two people

Playwright runs against node build/index.js — the same process a deployment runs — on a database rebuilt from the seed before every run, in a desktop and a Pixel 7 profile, and the design’s checks in a third at 360px. Six suites cover a stranger, an account, one trip’s every tab, the map’s own behaviour, two browsers on one trip, and invites plus the embed; a seventh asks every screen of the design, in both themes and at three widths, whether anything sticks out, whether a finger can hit it, what axe finds, and how it paints, on a fast connection and a slow one; and a bundle guard after the build holds the chunks to a budget. How the suite is kept honest, what it found, and what each failure taught.

By the end of this chapter

Run the end-to-end suite locally, read a failure’s call log and trace, and write a new test that signs in, does one thing, and cleans up after itself.

An end-to-end test is the only kind that can fail because of a seam: a cookie the hook did not read, a header the adapter did not send, a prerendered page that baked the wrong user in, a form the CSRF check refused. Those are exactly the failures that unit tests cannot see and that real people hit first. So the suite runs against the *built* application — the adapter’s output, its server, its database — and not against the dev server, and the configuration says why at length.

Read the webServer block as a recipe: rebuild the database from the migrations and the seed, build the app, start the adapter’s server on port 4173. Playwright waits for the port, runs the suite, and stops the process. reuseExistingServer is on outside CI, so a developer who already has the built server running skips the three-minute build — and in CI it is off, so the pipeline always tests what it just built. The environment block matters more than it looks: PUBLIC_ORIGIN is baked into the bundle at build time (chapter 03), and the server compares it with each request’s origin; if the build said 5173 and the test hits 4173, every form submission is a 403. It took an afternoon to learn that the same value has to be present in both places, which is why the comment is there.

workers: 1 and fullyParallel: false are not timidity. The suite shares one SQLite file and its tests *create* things — a trip, a stop, an expense — and then expect to find them; two workers would race. Serial costs several minutes of wall clock for two hundred and forty-one tests across the three projects — the design suite’s axe runs are most of it — plus the build, the first time, and buys a suite whose failures are always real. The third project is the Pixel 7 narrowed to 360px, with a screen of the same size, and it runs visual.e2e.ts alone: a behaviour does not change between 412px and 360px, and a layout does.

The database is deleted and rebuilt before every run — the file and its -wal and -shm sidecars — through the *migrations*, not drizzle-kit push. That is a small act of discipline with a large payoff: a schema change that was made in schema.ts and never turned into a migration fails here, on a developer’s machine, instead of in the container in chapter 44. The seed (chapter 13) then creates three people and two trips, and every test knows their names.

The helpers: what every test needs

signIn goes through the real form, not through an API call and a hand-made cookie: the test then exercises the sign-in remote form, the redirect guard and the session cookie’s attributes for free. openMenu is the phone-versus-desktop seam made explicit — the header’s links are behind a menu button under 48em — so a test written once runs unchanged in both projects. It waits for the root layout’s data-hydrated attribute first, because the menu button needs JavaScript and a click before hydration is a click nobody is listening to; the language-switch test found that one, about one run in twenty. openTab finds the tab strip by its accessible name and asserts the URL afterwards, because the tab *is* a URL (?tab=expenses) and a test that clicked a tab and moved on would not notice if the click had been swallowed.

typeDate exists because Bits UI’s date picker is not an <input type="date">; it is three editable segments per date, in the locale’s order, and Playwright’s fill() has nothing to fill. Clicking a segment and typing is what a person does, so it is what the helper does — and the work is in typeDateInto, which takes any date input as a locator, because the expense form’s date is the same picker now: the trip’s two dates find their input by position in the range, the expense finds its by role, getByRole("group", { name: "Date", exact: true }). When a control has a custom keyboard model, the helper that drives it belongs in one place with a comment saying what that model is.

Six suites

The stranger’s suite asserts things that are easy to break and hard to notice. That the guides page ships no script at all is the whole point of csr = false (chapter 34), and script[src] count zero is the only assertion that proves it. That /de/guides has lang="de" proves the reroute hook, the prerender entries and the %paraglide.lang% replacement all agree for a page that was built at compile time, with no request to consult. That the text inside a guide is Lisbon → Sintra with a distance proves a Svelte component inside Markdown ran the geodesy library at build time.

The same race as the sign-in form’s, on a plain input. Text typed into the explore filter before the page had hydrated was wiped when it did: the filter is a bind:value on a $state that starts empty, and hydration writes the state into the input. The account suite’s test of an explore-to-new-trip journey filled the filter straight after goto and failed on a slow run with “1 place” never appearing — the field was empty in its snapshot. The cure is the one keepTyped() applies to the form (chapter 32): the page’s script runs while the server’s input is still on the page, so the filter’s state starts from what is in it. The test holds the client bundle back, types, lets it go, and expects the text and the filtered list to have survived.

A test with JavaScript switched off, because the bug it guards was invisible with it on. With SvelteKit’s default paths.relative, a server render’s resolve() answered ./explore, and Paraglide’s localizeHref made that a whole URL at the build’s origin — in every page the server sent and every prerendered guide (chapter 23). The browser then hydrated and redrew every link as a path, so nothing looked wrong to anybody with a working script. test.use({ javaScriptEnabled: false }) makes the page exactly the HTML the server sent, and the test asks it three things: the header’s link is the path /de/explore, the header marks it aria-current="page", and no link anywhere starts with http://localhost. The phone project hides the nav behind a menu, so the locators say includeHidden — the links are in the HTML whether or not they are on screen, and the HTML is what is being tested.

And a test for the browser’s own handleError (chapter 14), which nothing else reaches: a remote function’s refusal goes through the server’s hook, so a page could lose its client hook and every other test would still pass. The globe is the one chunk loaded on demand, so the test drops it — page.route fetches each script and aborts the one that contains the globe’s class name, because the file’s own name is a hash — and opens the globe tab on a German page. The boundary must say “Etwas ist schiefgelaufen” with its “Neu verbinden” button, and the console must carry the hook’s [meridian] line. Without the hook, SvelteKit’s default fills the boundary with Internal Error, in English, and the first assertion fails.

The machine-facing test uses request — Playwright’s API client, with no browser — for the health endpoint and the route API, and the page for the embed frame. The interesting assertions are the negative ones: the private trip’s API is a 404, the private trip’s frame is a 404, and the public frame’s Content-Security-Policy contains frame-ancestors * — the one route the hook allows to be framed (chapter 43). A security rule with no test is a security rule that will be refactored away. The last two lines guard a different kind of seam: the frame ships no script, so nothing at run time would notice if it shipped no *style* either — and for a while it did, because a compiler option meant for the custom element caught this page too (chapter 36). They ask for two facts only the page’s own stylesheet makes true: the card’s computed max-width is the 22rem the CSS says, and its list has no indent. The first version asked whether *a* stylesheet was linked, and the root layout’s CSS is linked on every page — so the assertion was true with the bug as well. An assertion that cannot fail is a comment with a cost.

A fresh account with a unique email per run, so the test can run twice against the same database. It walks the whole loop — refused at /trips, sent to sign in with redirectTo remembered, creates the account, lands on an empty trips page, signs out, signs back in — and the openMenu calls are the phone project earning its keep. The two assertions on the header’s “Trips” link are about a page that did not reload: the header was drawn on the sign-in page, signed out, and the person is now signed in. They failed against a header whose link list was a bare {const}, worked out once (chapter 23).

The German test is about which code produced a sentence, not about German. The sign-in *handler*’s message — “that email and password do not match” — was always localised, because it is written with m.*() in the handler. The *schema*’s message for a malformed email runs before the handler, and it answered in English on every page until two things changed: the messages became functions called at failure time (chapter 12), and the Paraglide middleware read the locale from the page the form is on rather than the /_app/remote URL it posts to (chapter 20). The test asserts both halves — the German sentence is there, the English one is not — because a test that only looked for German would pass on a page that printed both.

The delete test answers the dialog twice. Playwright accepts nothing by default — a confirm() with no handler is dismissed — so page.once('dialog', …) decides each answer explicitly. First “Cancel”: the page must still be the settings page and the trip must still be in the list. Then “OK”: the trip must be gone. The first half is new, and it is new because it failed: the confirm() lived in an onsubmit that called preventDefault(), the remote form’s own submit listener does not look at defaultPrevented, and Cancel deleted the trip (chapter 31). Testing only the “yes” path of a question is testing half of it.

Two tests for things that used to go wrong without a sound. The first needs the server to refuse something the page asked for, and nothing on the trips list ever asks for anything wrong — so the test rewrites the request on its way out. page.route holds the tripPreview batch, swaps every argument for one the schema refuses, and lets it go on; the server’s handleError answers with its sentence for a failed validation, and the boundary must print it. *Where* it is printed is half of the assertion. +error.svelte shows page.error.message too, so a test that looked for the sentence anywhere on the page would still pass with the boundary gone and the whole page swapped for the error page. So the test looks inside the trips page: under its “Your trips” heading, in the snippet’s .issue paragraph, beside the Reconnect button that runs reset, where only the failed snippet can have put it. Against the old failed snippet the page said [object Object] (chapter 33). The second presses Refresh on the diagnostics page and expects the newest row to change, which it did not while the report was a bare {const} (chapter 35). Neither waits longer than the default: each change happens once a single request comes back.

beforeEach signs Ana in straight to her trip, and the first test presses ControlOrMeta+k — Playwright’s name for “Control on Linux and Windows, Command on a Mac” — to open the command palette and jump to a tab by typing part of its name. A keyboard shortcut is a feature people rely on and never think to report when it breaks.

The expenses test adds one row and asserts a *consequence*: that the settle-up now says Ben pays Ana. Its date used to be fill("2026-05-10") on a native date input; the field became the segmented picker, in the page’s language rather than the browser’s, so the test types the date segment by segment like a person — the same assertion, through the control that ships. It then removes the row, so the next test — and the next run against a reused server — starts from the seed. Tests that clean up after themselves are the alternative to a database reset between every test, which would cost seconds each and would hide any test that depended on the order.

The map has a suite of its own because its three bugs were behaviours a screenshot cannot show. The first is a click that goes two places: for an editor a click on the map starts a stop, and pressing a bubble opened the “New stop” dialog over the zoom it asked for (chapter 27 explains the event delegation behind it). The test presses a bubble and then a pin and expects no dialog, and then clicks the map itself and expects one — the second half is what keeps the first from passing by breaking clicks altogether. markers() runs in the page and reads every marker’s centre by its label, which is what the other two tests compare.

The second is a camera that was taken back. Choosing a stop flew the map to it, and the live query’s next snapshot — brought by the heartbeat the choice itself sends — re-fitted the whole route a few frames later. The test chooses Sagrada Família on the desktop’s side map, waits past the flight and the heartbeat, and expects the chosen pin in the middle of the map. Not Madrid, which was the first choice and is the lesson: Madrid is near the middle of the route, so a re-fit put its pin within a few pixels of the centre too, and the test passed against the bug. A test of “it went there” needs a there that nothing else would go to. The third is pins out of place: a resize at rest makes MapLibre place every marker afresh, so after a one-pixel round trip of the window no marker may have moved — against the bug, the Lisbon bubble moved 24px.

This is the test the project was built to pass. browser.newContext() twice gives two independent browser profiles — two cookie jars, two sessions — in one test. Ana and Ben sign in separately, and everything after that is a statement about the live query (chapter 18): Ben adds a stop and *Ana’s page* shows it, without a reload, because both pages hold the same query.live open and the server publishes to the room when the trip changes. The presence assertions ride on the same stream — Ana sees Ben arrive, and sees which stop he is looking at. The timeouts are longer than the default, deliberately: the presence heartbeat is fifteen seconds apart, and a test that asserts within five would be asserting on luck.

The second test uses the two people for something else: a command the server refuses for a real reason. Ben adds Bilbao, a stop the seed does not have, so no other test loses a row it counts on, and opens it to rename it; Ana removes it — after a reload, so nothing waits on the live query; Ben saves, and updateStop answers 404. What the browser’s await rejects with is the HttpError SvelteKit rebuilt from the answer, with the server’s sentence on body.message, and the toast must say it — “That stop is no longer on the trip.”, a Paraglide message (chapter 20) — and say nothing else. The assertion is on the toast’s whole title, toHaveText, and that is the point of the test. Its first version looked for the toast { hasText: 'Not found' }, and hasText matches a part of the text: the toast the old code printed, String(error), was {"status":404,"message":"Not found"}, which *contains* the words, so the test passed against the very bug errorMessage was written to fix (chapter 25). Run against String(error) now, it fails, with the JSON in the call log.

The third is about a bug only a second person could cause. The note’s editor was built by an attachment that read the live document, so every snapshot of the live query destroyed the editor and built a new one (chapter 30). A snapshot cannot be waited for directly, but its consequence can: the presence chip is drawn from the same snapshot as the document, so once Ben is on Ana’s screen, Ana’s page has applied a snapshot after her save. Then the test types again *without clicking* — toBeFocused first, because an editor that was rebuilt has lost the cursor, and the keystrokes after it go nowhere — and reloads to prove both sentences reached the server. The old notes test typed once and waited for “Saved”, which the bug never touched.

The settings test has a shape worth copying: try … finally. It flips the trip to visible-by-link, checks that the embed section appears and that the custom element inside it renders the trip *through the route API* — Playwright locators pierce shadow DOM, so page.locator('meridian-route').getByText(…) reaches inside — and then, whatever happened, flips it back. Without the finally, one failure in the middle would leave the seeded trip public, and the stranger’s suite in the next run would fail on a 200 where it expects a 404, two files away from the cause.

The suite that looks at the design

The six suites above are about behaviour. The seventh, visual.e2e.ts, is about the things a person reviewing a screenshot is bad at: a control that runs two pixels past its card, a button a finger cannot hit, a missing accessible name, a colour pair a theme change broke. It walks the same list of screens scripts/screens.ts photographs — one list, so the screens a person reviews are the screens the gate checks.

A screen is a URL plus whatever has to happen before it is the screen: a filter that matches nothing, a sign-in with a bad email, the stop dialog open, the palette, a toast, the phone’s open menu. Twenty-seven of them, in both themes, in all three projects. ALLOWED_SCROLLERS names the elements that are wider than the screen on purpose — the expenses table’s wrapper, the tab strip, the two canvases, the toaster, the closed nav — so the overflow check can tell a scroller from a leak.

The checks are functions that run *in the page*: page.evaluate(fn, arg) sends a function’s source text to the browser and calls it there, so each must be self-contained — no imports, nothing from the module scope, everything it needs as its one argument. The overflow check asks two questions. Does anything end past the right edge of the screen, outside an allowed scroller? And does any form control run past its card’s *content box*? The second exists because the first missed a real bug: at 360px the new-trip date field poked through the card’s padding onto its border, which does not widen the page, so scrollWidth was fine and the field was not. And the gate missed it a second way, which is why there is a third project: the overflow walk ran on the desktop and on a 412px phone, the bug was there only at 360px, and a review that put the fix back to the broken CSS found the suite still green. A check that runs at the wrong width is a check of a different page.

The target check is the design’s rule made executable: on a phone, every visible button, link, input, select, option and role="button" is drawn at least 36px each way and answers a press anywhere in a 44px box around its centre. The second half is asked of the browser itself — document.elementFromPoint() just inside each edge of that box — so a ::after that extends the hit area counts, and a neighbour drawn over it does not. A checkbox inside a <label> is measured as its label, because the label is what a finger presses; a link inside a sentence is exempt, as WCAG 2.5.8 exempts it; with a modal open only the dialog is swept, because everything behind it is under the scrim on purpose; and a toast passing over the page is a moment, not a layout. Each element is scrolled to the middle of the screen first, so the sticky header is never what the probe hits.

role="button" is in the list because of the map. A MapLibre marker is a div with that role, and the probe used to sweep only real buttons, links and form controls — so the pins and the bubbles were checked by nothing, and a mutation that shrank every pin to 16px left the check green. With them in, it found the pins’ press area was 40px, from the same padding-edge arithmetic as the icon buttons (chapter 27). A marker is the second, and narrowest, exemption: it may be *drawn* down to WCAG’s own 24px, because a pin is 26px so the route under it stays readable — that is the map’s legibility, not its target — and it must still answer the full 44px press. A marker is never scrolled itself, because scrolling inside a map would move the picture under the probe; its map is brought to the middle instead, and a marker outside what its map shows is not on the screen to press.

Its first run failed on controls that *looked* right, and both reasons are worth knowing. An absolutely positioned ::after with inset: -4px is measured from the element’s *padding box*, so on a 36px button with a 1px border it reached 42px, not 44 — hence --reach in base.css, which is half the difference plus the border. And two 36px buttons 8px apart, on a phone whose device pixel ratio is 2.625, met at a seam that rounds to one device pixel or the other; a press exactly between them could land on either, so the gaps between adjacent small targets became 12px, and a segmented control on a touch screen became 44px tall. Neither shows in a screenshot.

Signing in afresh for every signed-in screen would be over eighty sign-ins — fourteen screens, two themes, three projects. test.extend adds two fixtures: anaState, scoped to the *worker*, signs Ana in once through the real form and saves the cookies as a storage-state file; and signedIn, an *option* a describe block sets with use(). The built-in storageState fixture is then overridden to read one from the other, so each test gets a fresh context that starts signed in or signed out, as its screen says — and still a real session, made by the real form.

axe is the engine behind most accessibility tooling, and @axe-core/playwright runs it in a Playwright page. Two choices are deliberate. The engine is the project’s own axe-core, read from node_modules and handed over as axeSource, so the rules are the newest release rather than whichever the adapter bundled. And every rule axe tags wcag2a or wcag2aa — WCAG 2’s Level A and AA — runs, and *any* violation fails — not “no serious ones”, which is how a suite learns to live with a moderate problem forever. Only the two canvases are excluded, because a WebGL picture is not something axe can read — the canvases and nothing else. The first version excluded MapLibre’s .maplibregl-canvas-container, the element the canvas sits in, and every marker sits in it too: a dozen buttons people press, with names a screen reader announces, were out of axe’s sight, and stripping their names changed nothing in the result. Now it is canvas.maplibregl-canvas, and axe reads the markers like any other button. One rule has an exception, on one selector, with the reason written beside it: the palette’s list scrolls and focus never enters it, because it is the listbox of a combobox driven from the input with aria-activedescendant, and a tab stop there would do nothing. So the main run disables that rule and a second run applies it to the whole page *except* that selector — an exception that cannot quietly widen.

The whole matrix runs with reducedMotion: 'reduce', and the comment says why: the questions are about where a screen settles. The first run found a 1.97:1 primary button on the dark home page — axe had measured it at 97% opacity, half way through the hero’s fade. Motion is checked where it is decided, in the tokens that reduced motion zeroes; the matrix checks the page it settles into.

Why both axe and a hand-written target check

Because axe’s target-size rule is WCAG 2.2’s 2.5.8 — 24px, with spacing — and is not among the rules this suite runs, which are the ones axe tags wcag2a and wcag2aa. The design asks for more — 36px drawn and 44px to press on a phone, the platform guidelines’ number — and no off-the-shelf rule knows the brief. The general tool checks the standard; the probe above checks the promise the design made. When a project’s own rules are stricter than the standard, they need their own test, or they are a wish.

One map at any width. The itinerary’s side map exists from 64em and not below, and the reason is a WebGL context: a hidden MapLibre is still one, and a phone would pay for two on the Map tab. The test opens the itinerary at 1440px and counts one canvas, narrows the same page to 700px and counts none, widens it again and counts one — the MediaQuery that decides it is live, so resizing mounts and unmounts the map — and then on the Map tab counts one at both widths.

And the three pages people land on — home, explore, a public trip — are measured on the phone profile, twice, with PerformanceObservers installed before any of the page’s own script runs. buffered: true delivers the entries that happened before the observer existed. The first time the page loads as it is, and Cumulative Layout Shift must be *zero*, not under Lighthouse’s 0.1; when it is not, the test prints what moved, from each shift’s sources. The wait before reading is a second and a half, long enough for anything late — a chart, the live chip, a font — to have moved if it was going to.

The second time it loads over a slow connection, and the largest paint must still land inside 2.5 seconds. Unthrottled, on the machine running the suite, that budget meant nothing: the home page’s largest paint was 0.36 seconds and would have had to get seven times worse to fail. So a CDP session — Chromium’s DevTools protocol, which Playwright opens for any page — applies Network.emulateNetworkConditions with the round trip and bandwidth Lighthouse’s mobile preset assumes: 150ms, 1.6 Mbps down, 750 kbps up. The home page’s hero then paints at 2.27 seconds, within twenty milliseconds on every run, because a throttled network is the same network everywhere. That is a gate with 230ms of headroom: about forty kilobytes more in front of the hero, and it fails.

Why throttle the connection and not the processor

Because a CPU multiplier is relative to the machine it runs on: “four times slower” is one speed on a laptop and another on a CI runner, so the same test would mean two different things. A throttled connection is a fixed number of milliseconds and bytes per second wherever it runs — and here it is the network that decides, too: adding the 4× CPU slowdown on top moved the home page’s paint by less than the run-to-run spread. It is not Lighthouse’s own figure, and the comment says so: Lighthouse simulates each request from an unthrottled run, and its preset for applied throttling adds a margin for that, 562.5ms round trips. On that preset this server’s home page paints at 6.1 seconds: the hero is requested in the first 700ms and arrives last, behind forty module preloads sharing HTTP/1.1’s six connections to one host. A reverse proxy that speaks HTTP/2 in front of node build would change that number, and chapter 44’s compose file leaves room for one. The gate holds the number it can hold steadily, and the other is written down here so that nobody mistakes one for the other.

Why zero, when 0.1 is “good”

Because this project can have zero, and a threshold invites spending it. Every image has its width and height, the fonts are preloaded, the live chip’s slot is as wide as its widest label, the charts reserve their boxes. A shift here would be a bug with a cause, and 0.05 of budget would let the first one through unnoticed and the second one argue it was only another 0.05. A field measurement of real visitors is the place for thresholds; a lab test of three known pages is the place for zero.

The pictures are still taken, and still looked at by a person — this suite does not replace a review, it holds the review’s conclusions. scripts/screens.ts walks the same matrix in three viewports — the 1440×900 desktop, the Pixel 7, and a 360px phone, the narrowest width the type scale is tuned for — and two themes, writes a PNG of each screen to design/screens/, and prints the overflow and contrast reports beside them from the same two modules the gates use — exiting non-zero on a problem of either kind. The design of this app was reviewed that way, three times, a hundred-odd pictures at a time; every finding that a machine could have made is now one of the checks above — the third review was largely of the checks themselves, and found the two blind spots this chapter describes — and the ones it could not — a heading that wrapped badly, a fade in the wrong place — are in the comments beside the CSS that fixed them. The folder is ignored by git, because the pictures change with every CSS edit and a few megabytes of PNGs in every diff would bury the change itself.

The bundle guard

Two rules of the design can break while every test passes: GSAP belongs in the home page’s chunk and nowhere else, and no chunk over 20 KB gzipped may appear without somebody agreeing to it. A build that succeeds says nothing about either. So pnpm run verify runs node scripts/bundle-guard.ts between the build and the end-to-end suite, and the guard needs to know what is in each chunk — which a hashed file name does not say.

The bundler knows. A Vite plugin is an object with hooks, and generateBundle is called once per environment with every chunk the build is about to write, including the modules in each and how many bytes of each survived into the output (renderedLength). SvelteKit’s build has a client environment and a server one; the plugin writes only the client’s, to .svelte-kit/bundle-stats.json — beside the build, never in it, so it is not served.

A budget keyed by file name would break on every edit, because the hash changes with the content. So each chunk is *named* by what it is: the route it renders, the module it was split at (the globe’s dynamic import), or the package that is most of it — names that survive an edit. Two chunks of one package get the largest module’s path inside the package after the name, without pnpm’s version-stamped store path, so an upgrade does not rename them either.

Five chunks are over the limit and all five are in scripts/bundle-budget.json, with the size they were measured at — three of them a little over it since, which is what the 10% is for. The trip page is big because it is MapLibre, Tiptap and LayerChart; the globe is three.js, and it loads only when somebody opens that tab (chapter 28). A budgeted chunk may grow 10% before the guard fails; a new chunk over 20 KB fails at once, with its name and its size. When a change is meant to grow one, --write measures again and rewrites the budget — and the budget is a file in the repository, so the growth is a line in the diff that a reviewer sees.

Why a budget in a file, and not a limit in the config

Vite’s chunkSizeWarningLimit is one number for every chunk, a warning, and it is either too low for the trip page or too high for everything else. A budget per named chunk says something more useful: *this* chunk is big, on purpose, at *this* size. It makes the decision visible, and it turns a slow drift — a dependency that adds 3 KB a month — into a failure on the day it crosses 10%, rather than a discovery a year later.

What the suite found

A suite is worth what it catches. Before it went green this one caught six bugs that no unit test could have — one of them only in the phone project, one only in about one run in ten, and one that had been hiding behind a .catch(() => {}), which is the argument for a phone project and for never dismissing a flaky test in one paragraph.

  1. The trip page was a 500 for signed-in members. An $effect that sent the presence heartbeat read the heartbeat command’s own pending state, which the command updates synchronously — an effect that re-triggers itself, and Svelte stopped it with effect_update_depth_exceeded. The fix is in chapter 24: read the trip id once, and wrap the command call in untrack. The desktop test found this in the first run; the pages had looked fine in a browser because the stack trace was in the server log.
  2. The place search never searched. Bits UI’s Combobox.Input is a controlled input; binding its value is not the same as listening to it, and the query the component filtered on was never updated. Nobody noticed by hand because the seeded stops were already there. pressSequentially in the test — typing a character at a time, as a person does — found it.
  3. The settings page did not update after Save. The command used .updates(tripBySlug(slug)) so the server sent the refreshed trip in the same response, and the cache was set — but the page read the query through an await in the markup that was worked out once and kept its first answer — a bare {const initial = await query}, in today’s syntax. {const initial = $derived(await query)} follows the query, and chapter 31 shows the page reading it once, that way, with nothing beside it to keep in step.
  4. Text typed before the page had hydrated vanished. One run in ten, the sign-in helper filled the email, clicked, and nothing happened: the trace showed no request at all, and the screenshot showed an empty email field with the browser’s “Please fill out this field” bubble under it. Playwright had typed faster than the client bundle loaded, and when the remote form hydrated, its field wrote its *own* value — the empty string the server rendered — over the typed one. That is a real bug for a person on a slow connection, not a test artefact. The fix is keepTyped() in chapter 32: read the inputs before the template hydrates and make what is there the field’s value. The test that pins it holds the client bundle back with page.route, types, releases it, and waits for a data-hydrated attribute the root layout sets in onMount before asserting the text is still there.
  5. The seed’s ids were not ids. Ben clicked a seeded stop and Ana never saw him move to it, while a stop Ben had just added worked perfectly. The seed built its ids by hand — 00000000-0000-4000-8000-0000000a001 — and the last group was one character short of a UUID, so the presence heartbeat naming that stop failed the IdSchema check on the server, and the client’s .catch(() => {}) on a fire-and-forget command swallowed the error. Every command that names a seeded row — remove this stop, edit that expense — was failing the same way, silently. The fix is in chapter 13: seedId() builds the fixed ids *through the schema*, so a malformed one throws at seed time instead of vanishing at run time. The lesson is older than the bug: the data you seed must pass the validation you run.
  6. On a phone, the Add-an-expense button could not be clicked. Playwright’s call log said <h3> intercepts pointer events — the button was where it should be, and the click landed somewhere else. The cause was two layers down: the expenses table is seven columns wide, the page’s grid column was implicitly auto, and an auto track will not be narrower than its content, so the whole page was 711 pixels wide on a 412-pixel screen. Mobile Chromium reacts to a page wider than the viewport by laying it out at a larger *layout* viewport, and Playwright’s coordinates and the browser’s stopped agreeing. grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) on the page grid, and the table scrolls inside its wrapper as it was meant to. The suite found a real mobile layout bug by failing to press a button.

The last one is the reason to be suspicious of “element is not stable” and “intercepts pointer events” in a mobile project. They usually mean the *page* is wrong, not the test, and the useful next step is to measure document.documentElement.scrollWidth against clientWidth on that page. The same probe ran across every route afterwards, in both languages, and the expenses tab was the only offender. That probe is now overflowInPage, and it runs on every screen in the matrix.

The design suite’s first run, against screens that had already passed a review by eye, added four more: hit areas of 42px where the CSS said 44, because an ::after is measured from the padding box; presses that could land on either of two buttons 8px apart at a fractional device pixel ratio; a primary button at 1.97:1, measured by axe half way through a fade; and the palette’s list, a scrollable region with no tab stop, which turned out to be right and became the one written exception. And the behaviour suites, re-run, found the two that started this round: Cancel on “Delete this trip?” deleted the trip, and a German form answered in English. Each is now a test, so each is found once.

Then a review of the gates themselves. It changed the code under each check to the broken version and watched for red, and found checks that were looking away: the overflow walk never ran at 360px, where its own bug lived; axe and the target probe never saw the map’s markers; the embed’s stylesheet assertion was true with the bug. Pointed at the map, the new suite found three bugs the pictures could not show — a bubble press that also started a stop, a flight taken back by a heartbeat, and pins 25px from the route on a phone — and the account suite, failing once in a slow run, found the explore filter wiping what was typed before hydration. The method is the lesson: a test is only known to work once it has been seen to fail.

The latest review read the code against the documentation and found three more, each of which every existing test had passed: a notes editor that a companion’s arrival destroyed mid-sentence; links in the server’s HTML that were whole URLs at the build’s origin, so the header never marked the page it was on until a script redrew it; and a toast test whose hasText was satisfied by the JSON dump it existed to prevent. Each new test above was then run against the old code — the attachment without untrack, paths.relative back at its default, String(error) in the toast, the client hook removed — and seen to fail before it was trusted.

When a test fails, test-results/<test>/ holds a screenshot, an error-context.md with the accessibility tree at the moment of failure, and a trace.zip — open it with pnpm exec playwright show-trace <file> for a timeline with every action, every network request and a DOM snapshot at each step. The trace is almost always faster than a debugger.

Checkpoint

  • You can explain why the suite runs against node build/index.js and what PUBLIC_ORIGIN has to do with a 403.
  • You can write a two-context test and say which assertion in it proves the live query rather than a reload.
  • You can read a Playwright call log that says “intercepts pointer events” and name the first thing to measure.
  • You can say what the target check asks the browser that a measurement of the box cannot, and how an axe exception is kept to one selector.
  • You can say why the design’s checks run at 360px as well as 412px, and why the throttled test slows the connection and not the processor.
  • You can describe how to prove a test can fail, and name an assertion in this chapter that could not.
  • You can explain how the bundle guard names a chunk, and what has to change in the repository for a budgeted chunk to grow.
